newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soybeans end slightly up on wheat limit gains.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soybeans end slightly up on wheat limit gains.

text.p: CBOT soybeans ended a choppy session higher with support coming from wheat futures which were locked limit up most of the day, traders said.
But the upside was limited by follow-through selling from Friday's near-limit losses tied to bearish technical signals and ideas soybeans had risen enough to ration demand.
Wheat opened with 20-cent-per-bushel limit gains and closed locked limit up on reports a weekend freeze in key hard red winter wheat growing areas likely caused widespread damage.
Floor sources noted increased buying interest in soybeans and corn after wheat locked limit up.

Weather was also deemed bearish for soybeans. Forecasts called for continued cool weather across the U.S. Midwest, adding to concerns corn plantings would be delayed. Soybeans can be planted later than corn.

"The soybean market also is dampened by the fact that we haven't had ideal planting conditions in the spring wheat belt or the Corn Belt so far," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities. "That's why we're so choppy in here."
Soybeans ended 3-3/4 to one cent per bushel higher with May up 2-1/2 at $8.33 and new crop November up 2-1/4 at $7.04-1/4.
But the technical outlook remained bleak, chartists said.

Soybeans traded on both sides Monday as bearish technicals battled with bullish underlying fundamentals, pit sources said. Some traders said Friday's near-limit losses completed a "head-and-shoulders" chart formation which is considered a bearish signal.
But fundamental traders continued to look at USDA's ending stocks projection for a tight 125 million bushels, the lowest level in 20 years.

They also noted Safras e Mercado on Monday cut its outlook for Brazilian soybean production to 26.22 million tonnes from 26.88 million. Safras said drought cut 700,000 tonnes off production in Rio Grande do Sul.

On the day, funds were mostly buyers of new crop November but sellers of the old crop months, traders said. Griffin Trading bought seven million bushels November while Smith Barney sold three million May, 3.5 million July and two million November, pit sources said.
Refco Inc spread four million bushels July/May at six to 6-1/4 cents and Smith Barney spread two million bushels May/July at six cents, traders said.
In options trade, Griffin Trading sold 1,000 November $8.75 calls at 20 cents and Goldenberg-Hehmeyer sold 600 July $8.50 calls at 33 cents, floor sources said.
Soybean volume was estimated by CBOT at 88,000 contracts, compared with Friday's actual volume of 103,057 contracts.
